tagline.text: A multi-tiered waterfall deep in the Maragusan highlands, reached by rope climbs and a squeeze between boulders

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangays Coronobe and Mapawa area, Maragusan, Davao de Oro

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800~2,500 (per person from Davao, transport and meals included, guide tip not included, 1–2 days)

children.text: Pyalitan Falls is a multi-tiered waterfall in the highlands of Maragusan, Davao de Oro. There is no entrance fee, but river crossings, rope climbs and a tight squeeze between boulders make it the hardest and most scenic of Maragusan's waterfall trails.
Pyalitan Falls lies in the mountains of Maragusan, in Davao de Oro (formerly Compostela Valley) in southeastern Mindanao. The provincial tourism website puts it about
7 km

northeast of the Maragusan town proper (poblacion), and OpenStreetMap marks the falls at roughly 7.30 degrees north, 126.17 degrees east, inside Barangay Coronobe. Some guides say Barangay Mapawa and others name a different barangay for the jump-off, so rather than worrying about the exact administrative boundary, just remember it as the falls you reach by motorcycle or tricycle from Maragusan town. The area is a highland at about
above sea level, so the air is much cooler than in Davao City.

What defines this waterfall is how demanding the route is. Tagbibinta, another Maragusan waterfall, has concrete steps and railings, but Pyalitan means walking in from the jump-off through mud, tall grass, narrow cliffside paths, river crossings and a big boulder you climb with a rope. One travel blogger called it the hardest and most beautiful trail, and another wrote that you climb a small rock wall at the first cascade and then go up a wooden ladder and squeeze through a narrow gap between boulders at the second. In exchange, there are few visitors and the payoff on arrival is large.

Sources disagree on the size of the falls. One blog describes a four-tier waterfall whose highest tier is about 150 feet, another mentions a waterfall about 46 meters high with a deep catch basin, and a Maragusan weekend guide estimated about 200 feet across all tiers. The provincial tourism site describes nine tiers and about 120 feet. The numbers seem to depend on how many tiers are counted and how far up each writer climbed, so rather than trusting any single height, think of it as a large waterfall made up of many tiers. Cold, clear mountain water drops into the deep pool beneath the highest tier.

The first thing to remember when planning is that this is not an easy sightseeing stop. There is no entrance fee and no store, and even though the trail is established, some sections become dangerous in the rain. The safest approach is to contact the Maragusan tourism office first, check the current trail condition and get a guide referral. A day trip from Davao involves a long journey, so many travelers stay a night in Maragusan and combine it with the sea of clouds at Calamba Farm, Tagbibinta Falls and Marangig Falls.

blocks.title: Rope climb at the first tier

children.text: The first section near the falls is a small rock wall with water rushing beside it. You have to climb using a rope or ladder, and the wet rock is slippery. If it is your first time, watch where your guide or the people ahead put their feet and follow slowly. It is best not to attempt it when the water is high.

The next section has a large makeshift wooden ladder, and above it you have to squeeze through a gap between boulders. One account says the gap is barely wide enough for an adult, so it is safer to hold a large backpack in front of you or hand it to your guide. People with a larger build or claustrophobia should know this beforehand.

Depending on the source, the highest tier is described as about 46 meters or about 150 feet. The water dropping into a deep pool and the roar echoing in the narrow gorge are the highlight of this trail. The water looks clearest when midday sunlight reaches it.

Part of the route crosses or follows the stream flowing down from the falls. Choose the shallow spots to cross, as the stones are slippery with moss. Warnings not to cross right after rain come up again and again, because the water level can rise suddenly. Water shoes with a firm sole are more comfortable than sandals.

The trail passes through mud, tall grass and cliffside paths, with dense forest and valley views along the way. Maragusan sits at a high elevation and stays relatively cool even at midday, so trekking here is much less tiring than in the usual Philippine heat. For landscape photos, the morning after the clouds clear is best.

Tagbibinta, close to town, is a waterfall improved with steps; Marangig is a quiet waterfall reached by a river trek of about 20 minutes; and Pyalitan is described as the farthest and hardest. Choose according to your stamina and time, and putting the toughest trail last makes the schedule easier to plan.

blocks.title: A natural waterfall with no entrance fee

children.text: Several guides say there is no entrance fee. There are almost no facilities, so do not expect shops, stalls or changing rooms. Set aside money separately for the guide tip and motorcycle fare, and carry out all your trash.

blocks.title: Sunrise and highland scenery around Maragusan

children.text: Because the trip to Pyalitan alone is long, many travelers combine it with the sunrise sea of clouds at Calamba Farm. One report says to arrive around 4:30 a.m., that the clouds are clearest at 5–6 a.m. and thin out by about 7, so it works well to do the sea of clouds early in the morning and the waterfall in the afternoon.
Take a bus or van to Maragusan from the Davao Ecoland Terminal or the van terminal next to Gaisano Mall Bajada. Many guides say the ride takes about
4–5 hours
Arrive in Maragusan town, leave your bags at your lodging and have lunch. In the afternoon you can visit nearby Tagbibinta Falls.
Have dinner in town and rest early. Arrange the guide and motorcycle times for the next day in advance.
Go up to Calamba Farm before dawn to see the sunrise and the sea of clouds. The clouds are best in the early morning.
Warm up with a light trek at Marangig Falls or head straight to Pyalitan.
Walk in with your guide from the Pyalitan jump-off. Accounts of how long it takes to reach the falls, including the river crossing and rope climb, differ, from about
30 minutes to 1 hour
Return to town, grab a bite and catch a ride back to Davao. Check the last departure time in advance.
According to the guides, the last hour of the road is a narrow one-lane cliff road where rockfall is possible, so it is safer to be off the road before dark.

items.title: From Maragusan town to the falls

children.text: Go from town to the jump-off by motorcycle (habal-habal) or tricycle. The one-way fare cited is about

Accounts put the ride at about
20–30 minutes

One account says it takes about
1.5 hours

From Tagum, the provincial tourism site says it takes about

The Davao region has no distinct dry season and rain is possible all year. Maragusan is a highland, so it is cooler and often cloudy, which makes the weather hard to predict. The guides say the falls look best and the crossings are easier on a sunny day, so pick a clear day.
The most important thing is to avoid the days just after rain or during rain, because the river crossings and rope sections become dangerous. Ask your guide about the local weather the day before.

There is no lodging or restaurant around the falls, so people usually stay in Maragusan town. Resorts such as Haven's Peak, with a night view from the hill above town, are mentioned, and a bunk is known to cost about
per person and an eight-person room about
. Prices and booking methods change often, so check on their Facebook page.

Eat at restaurants in town, and prepare packed lunches, water and snacks for the falls in advance. Some accounts say there are no stores along the way. If you need Korean groceries, it is better to buy them in Davao City.

Contact the Maragusan tourism office first to check the current trail condition and arrange a guide. A tourism contact number appears in some guides, but it may change, so confirm the latest information.
There is no evidence that a guide is mandatory, but the route can be confusing and dangerous, so we strongly recommend going with one.
Wear water shoes with firm soles or trekking shoes, and put your phone and wallet in a waterproof dry bag.
Bring water, snacks and a raincoat, and carry out all your trash.
Start on a clear morning and cross the river before the afternoon rain.
Check the last departure time for the ride back in advance and leave some margin.
If you are starting from Davao, it is efficient to plan two days and one night combining the Calamba Farm sunrise and Tagbibinta Falls.
Transport and guide tips are often paid in cash, so bring some small bills in advance.
Do not cross rivers or climb rocks on rainy days or when the water is high. Guides repeatedly warn about slippery rock and rising water.
The rope climb at the first cascade and the narrow boulder gap require stamina and nerve, and there is a risk of accidents.
One account says the last hour of the road from Davao to Maragusan is a narrow one-lane cliff road where rockfall is possible. Avoid traveling at night.
Some accounts say there are no stores near the falls, so bring water and snacks.
Travel times and routes differ from source to source. The trail may have changed, so always follow your local guide.
Check the latest announcements before your visit on the security situation and any checkpoint requirements in the Maragusan area.
